title: Introducing Noema Issue VII: The Next Axial Age | NOEMA
gist: Noema editor Nathan Gardels frames the convergence of AI, synthetic biology and climate crisis as a potential 'New AI-xial Age' comparable to the original Axial Age (800-200 BCE), surveying thinkers who split on whether AI expands human and planetary self-understanding (Rees, Bratton) or instead produces an 'epistemic monoculture' and eventual loss of human centrality (Scharmer, Hinton, Lovelock).

insights.claim: Nathan Gardels argues that today's simultaneous crises in AI, synthetic biology and climate, combined with dwindling trust in traditional faiths and institutions, mirror the conditions (widespread war, loss of ontological security) that produced the original Axial Age (roughly 800-200 BCE), when Confucianism, Buddhism, Greek philosophy and Hebrew prophecy arose in relative simultaneity.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Frames AI/biotech/climate disruption as a unifying civilizational narrative rather than isolated sector stories — useful lens for reading how policy and cultural discourse may converge around AI governance in coming years.
insights.quote: With no shared ideational framework and dwindling trust in bequeathed faiths and institutions, humanity is being forced back to first principles.
insights.locator: opening framing, after the Karl Jaspers section

insights.claim: Gardels, drawing on philosopher Charles Taylor, describes written language as the 'first cloud technology' that enabled the original Axial Age by allowing people to reflect abstractly beyond immediate tribal experience — implying AI could play an equivalent civilizational role as the next symbolic/information technology.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Positions AI not just as a productivity tool but as a candidate for a civilization-defining information technology on the order of writing itself — a framing that could shape how AI is regulated and mythologized culturally.
insights.quote: the stored memories of the first cloud technology
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'For the philosopher Charles Taylor...'

insights.claim: Gardels argues that Western scientific and technological dominance since antiquity, spread first through imperialism and then globalization, produced 'multiple modernities' worldwide whose economic and ecological effects have now reconverged into a single set of contemporaneous global challenges.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Suggests AI and biotech risk/opportunity will be experienced as a synchronized global phenomenon rather than a Western-only trend, relevant to thinking about global (not just US/China) AI adoption and regulatory convergence.

themes.theme: AI as Planetary and Personal Mirror

insights.claim: Philosopher of technology Benjamin Bratton, as cited by Gardels, argues that AI-driven supercomputing simulations of Earth's past, present and future climate constitute a 'self-disclosure of Earth's intelligence and agency' — i.e., climate modeling itself is becoming a new form of planetary self-knowledge accomplished through computation.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Reinforces the strategic value of large-scale AI/compute investment in Earth-system and climate modeling as a distinct application category beyond commercial chatbots.
insights.quote: The models that we have of climate change are ones that emerge from supercomputing simulations of Earth's past, present and future. This is a self-disclosure of Earth's intelligence and agency, accomplished by thinking through and with a computational model.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'As the philosopher of technology Benjamin Bratton puts it...'

insights.claim: Philosopher Tobias Rees, as cited by Gardels, argues that a personal AI model with access to a person's full data trail (emails, messages, documents, voice memos, photos) could reveal that person's own behavioral and thought patterns to them in a way no human interlocutor can, functioning as an external mirror for self-transformation.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Articulates a product thesis for deeply personal-data-integrated AI assistants (life-logging + LLM analysis) as a self-understanding/therapy-adjacent category distinct from productivity AI.
insights.quote: AI has much more information available than we do, and it can access and work through this information faster than we can. It also can discover logical structures in data — patterns — where we see nothing.

themes.theme: Contrarian Take: AI as Epistemic Monoculture

insights.claim: Awareness-based action researcher Otto Scharmer, in an essay Gardels cites, contends that the current concentration of investment in AI is producing an 'epistemic monoculture' — a single computational way of knowing that treats the world as a set of objects — analogous to how industrial agriculture's chemical monocropping was short-term productive but long-term devastating to soil diversity.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: A direct counter-narrative to AI-capex bull cases: flags a civilizational/cultural risk thesis that could feed AI-skeptic policy and ESG-style critiques of concentrated AI investment.
insights.quote: Just as industrial agriculture replaced the diversity of the living soil with chemical fertilizers and crop monocultures — productive in the short term, devastating over time — the current AI moment is producing an epistemic monoculture.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'In his essay in this upcoming issue, awareness-based action researcher Otto Scharmer...'

insights.claim: Scharmer, as cited by Gardels, claims that of the trillions of dollars flowing into AI, almost none is directed at cultivating human capacities such as sensing, relating and sensemaking — which he calls 'soil depletion at a civilizational scale.'
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Implies a capital-allocation imbalance narrative (compute/model spend vs. 'human capacity' investment) that could become a talking point in AI governance and future-of-work debates, though no dollar figure is sourced.
insights.quote: the human side of the equation — the cultivation of sensing, relating and sensemaking — receives almost none of it. This is soil depletion at a civilizational scale.
insights.locator: same paragraph as the epistemic monoculture quote

themes.theme: Superintelligence and the Loss of Human Centrality

insights.claim: Geoffrey Hinton, cited by Gardels as the 'godfather of neural networks,' warns that machines will become smarter than humans just as humans became smarter than animals, and argues there is little historical precedent for a lesser intelligence escaping domination by a superior one.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: A high-profile AI-safety voice framing loss-of-control risk in stark historical-analogy terms; relevant to tracking AI-safety/alignment discourse that can move regulatory sentiment and AI-safety-focused investment.
insights.quote: We were once smarter than animals; now machines will be smarter than us. There is little evidence in history that lesser intelligences were ever able to escape domination by some superior intelligence.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'The so-called godfather of "neural networks," Geoffrey Hinton...'

insights.claim: Historian Yuval Noah Harari, quoted by Gardels, frames the current AI/synthetic-biology moment as civilizational-scale: humanity's capacity to create intelligence and life exceeding natural evolutionary limits marks an ending point analogous to how human history began with the invention of gods.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Signals the intellectual mainstreaming of 'humans becoming god-like creators' framing around generative AI and synthetic biology, shaping public and regulatory narrative around these technologies.
insights.quote: History began when humans invented gods, and will end when humans become gods.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'As the historian Yuval Noah Harari puts it...'

insights.claim: Gaia theorist James Lovelock, in his final book 'Novacene' as summarized by Gardels, envisioned a future where a superior AI-organized intelligence structures civilization into an ecologically efficient but totalitarian 'wasp hive' in which human autonomy is severely diminished.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: A dystopian counterweight to techno-optimist AI narratives worth flagging for scenario planning around AI governance and loss-of-human-agency risk.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'This is what Gaia theorist James Lovelock seemed to conclude...'

insights.claim: Gardels invokes Nobel laureate Ilya Prigogine's view that the future does not simply emerge from the past because present action is shaped by our image of the future, and pairs it with complexity scientist Stuart Kaufmann's framing that preserving humans' active role in co-evolution is a 'sacred' vocation — the article's implicit call for deliberate human agency in shaping AI/biotech outcomes rather than assuming technological determinism.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Underscores that the article's core argument is normative/agentic (humans should actively shape AI's trajectory) rather than purely descriptive — relevant framing for governance and policy advocacy angles.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'The Nobel laureate Ilya Prigogine once remarked...'

insights.claim: Gardels identifies three defining, contemporaneous global challenges facing all of humanity today: AI that can become smarter than humans, synthetic biology capable of creating life in the lab, and biosphere degradation that threatens the basis of all life on Earth.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Explicitly links AI and biotech disruption with climate risk as a single interconnected threat/opportunity complex rather than separate silos — useful for cross-sector scenario and risk framing.
insights.quote: AI that can be smarter than humans, synthetic biology that can create life in the lab, and the degradation of the biosphere that is the basis of all life on Earth.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Collectively, everyone on the planet today faces the same challenges...'

insights.claim: Gardels notes that renewed tension among great powers armed with weapons of mass destruction persists alongside the AI, synthetic-biology and climate transitions, implying geopolitical conflict risk compounds rather than sits separate from the technological disruption he describes.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Long-horizon scenario planning should weight great-power/WMD conflict risk alongside AI and biotech disruption rather than treating them as independent variables.
insights.quote: the menacing return of adversity among the great powers armed with weapons of mass destruction
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'To boot, violence, civil strife, wars...'
